why: One hash, one input, two implementations, two repositories — and until
this file nothing had ever compared them. `astra-plugin locale sync`
WRITES the digests in `locales.lock.json` (`digest` in
astra-plugin-cli/src/commands/locale.rs); `bot/lib/locales.mjs` in
astra-registry READS them (`englishDigest`). They were run against the
same English once and produced the same values, which is agreement by
luck: nothing compared them, so nothing could have noticed the day they
stopped agreeing.
What that costs is quiet and asymmetric. If the two diverge, either
every translation looks stale to the registry and every card silently
falls back to English while `astra-plugin check` reports the lock
fresh, or a genuinely stale translation is published as current. Both
read, from the author's side, as nothing happening.
So the two are held to a table instead of to each other, and the table
was not written by either of them: every `digest` below is what
coreutils `sha256sum` returns for the vector's exact UTF-8 bytes.
`testdata/locales/digest-handcheck.sh` re-derives all of them that way
on every CI run. Two programs that share a mistake can agree with each
other; they cannot agree with coreutils.
Read by astra-plugin-cli/src/commands/locale_tests.rs and by
checkLocaleDigestVectors in astra-registry/tools/validate.mjs. Coupling
C19, gap 9.
Every reader asserts a FLOOR on what it loaded before it asserts
anything else: an empty vector file must fail as an empty vector file,
not pass as a clean run.

how_to_read_this.rule: digest = the first 12 hex of sha256 over the EXACT English UTF-8 bytes. No normalisation, of either the English or the translation. Lower-case hex.
how_to_read_this.vectors: name -> { english: the exact string, digest: the expected 12 hex, catches: the change this vector exists to turn red }.
how_to_read_this.escaping: Every non-ASCII character is written as a \uXXXX escape and this file is 7-bit ASCII on purpose. A vector that can be silently renormalised by an editor, a transfer or a merge tool is a vector that stops testing what it says it tests — and Unicode normalisation is one of the two failures this table is for.
how_to_read_this.pairs: Five pairs must NOT collide: lf/crlf, case-upper/case-lower, nfc-e-acute/nfd-e-acute, nfc-short-i/nfd-short-i, empty/single-space. Each pair is one normalisation somebody could add to one side. A reader is free to assert this; the generator does.
how_to_read_this.adding_one: Add the vector, write `catches`, re-derive with digest-handcheck.sh — and then break the digest function on purpose and watch the new vector go red. A vector that has never failed is a vector that might be asserting nothing.

vectors.name: empty
vectors.catches: a reader that treats empty English as a miss and records nothing, or returns "" rather than a digest. Python alone once treated "" as a miss in the I18n SDKs

vectors.name: tab

vectors.name: lf
vectors.catches: the LF half of the pair below

vectors.name: crlf
vectors.catches: a newline normalisation: this MUST NOT equal `lf`. Git's own autocrlf is the reason a reader may be handed either

vectors.name: trailing-lf
vectors.catches: a reader that strips a trailing newline, which is what reading a file with `read_to_string().trim()` does

vectors.name: non-breaking-space
vectors.catches: a whitespace normalisation that reaches U+00A0 — a plain trim does not, a regex \s in JavaScript does

vectors.name: soft-hyphen
vectors.catches: an invisible-character strip. `unsafeDisplayText` exists in the registry and a digest that ran after it would be a different number

vectors.name: case-upper
vectors.catches: the pair below

vectors.name: case-lower
vectors.catches: a lowercasing: this MUST NOT equal `case-upper`

vectors.name: nfc-e-acute
vectors.catches: the NFC half of the pair below

vectors.name: nfd-e-acute
vectors.catches: NFC/NFD: this MUST NOT equal `nfc-e-acute`. JavaScript has String.normalize() and one call added anywhere is this gap's whole failure

vectors.name: nfc-short-i
vectors.catches: Russian `Kratkiy` with a composed U+0439 — the NFC half of the pair below

vectors.name: nfd-short-i
vectors.catches: the same word with U+0438 + combining breve. MUST NOT equal `nfc-short-i`. Russian is the language this system's plural families are written for, so this is the decomposition an author actually hits

vectors.name: cyrillic-card
vectors.catches: multi-byte UTF-8 that is not Latin

vectors.name: japanese-card
vectors.english: ローカライズ規則の検証用フィクスチャ
vectors.catches: three-byte UTF-8 throughout

vectors.name: arabic-rtl
vectors.catches: right-to-left text, which a bidi-aware sanitiser would rewrite

vectors.name: astral-emoji
vectors.catches: a surrogate pair. A JavaScript implementation that hashed UTF-16 code units, or sliced by .length before encoding, gets a different answer here and nowhere in the ASCII vectors

vectors.name: bom-prefixed
vectors.catches: a BOM strip. A locale file that arrives with one is a real thing; a digest computed after stripping it is a second rule nobody wrote down

vectors.name: nul-inside
vectors.catches: a C-string truncation, and any FFI boundary that introduces one

vectors.name: backslash-and-quote
vectors.catches: a double-unescape when this file is read: a reader that decodes the JSON twice gets a literal newline here and a different digest

vectors.name: brace-placeholders
vectors.catches: the substitution syntax the SDKs implement — a digest taken after interpolation rather than before

vectors.name: dollar-key
vectors.catches: the `$key` form the daemon resolves. A digest taken after resolution is a digest of a different string

vectors.name: angle-and-amp
vectors.catches: an HTML-escaping pass between reading and hashing
